intro: Wistman's Wood is the oak wood Dartmoor is famous for, about 3.5 hectares of low, twisted, moss-covered oaks among granite boulders above the West Dart, north of Two Bridges. Its oldest oaks appear to be 400 to 500 years old, and most stand no taller than 4.5 metres. It is a National Nature Reserve, and visitors are asked to stay on the paths around the edge and not to enter the wood. The walk from the Two Bridges car park takes about 25 minutes.
meta_description: Wistman's Wood on Dartmoor holds oaks 400 to 500 years old that rarely pass 4.5 metres. About 120 lichens, why it is seen from the path, and the walk in.
question_meta: How old is Wistman's Wood? Its oldest oaks appear to be 400 to 500 years old. Why they stay so low, what grows on them, and how to see it from the path.
question_answer: The oldest oaks in Wistman's Wood on Dartmoor appear to be 400 to 500 years old, according to Wikipedia's summary of the research. Most are no more than 4.5 metres tall. The wood covers about 3.5 hectares and is seen from the paths around its edge, since visitors are asked not to enter it.
question_context: Wistman's Wood grows at 380 to 410 metres on the open moor in the valley of the West Dart, in three groves known as North, Middle and South. Around 1620 it was described as oaks no taller than a man could reach the top of with his head, and most still rarely exceed 4.5 metres, with a few between six and 7.6. The oldest appear to be 400 to 500 years old, and an oak felled in 1866 proved to be about 168. Wikipedia describes the trees as mainly pedunculate oak with some rowan, while one walking guide calls them sessile. What makes the wood precious is less the oaks than what lives on them and on the boulders, about 120 species of lichen among the mosses. Feet damage both, which is why Natural England and the Dartmoor National Park Authority ask visitors to keep to the paths around the edge. The wood has been a Site of Special Scientific Interest since 1964 and belongs to the Duchy of Cornwall. A 2023 plan aims to reduce grazing and foot traffic and expand the wood by 2040.

faq.q: Can you walk into Wistman's Wood?
faq.a: Natural England and the Dartmoor National Park Authority ask visitors to follow the paths around the wood and not to enter it, because erosion damages the lichens and mosses. The view from the path at its edge is the way to see it.

faq.q: How do I get to Wistman's Wood?
faq.a: Park at Two Bridges on the B3357, opposite the Two Bridges Hotel, and walk north for about 25 minutes.

trees.story:
Around 1620 a visitor described the oaks of Wistman's Wood as no taller than a man could reach the top of with his head. Four centuries later most of them still rarely pass 4.5 metres. They grow at 380 to 410 metres up on the open moor above the West Dart, rooted among granite boulders, low, twisted and thick with moss.

This is a wood, not a tree, and the wood is the destination. It covers about 3.5 hectares in three groves, North, Middle and South. The oldest oaks appear to be 400 to 500 years old; one felled in 1866 turned out to be about 168. Wikipedia names them mainly pedunculate oak with some rowan, while one walking guide says sessile, so the exact species is less settled than the place.

What the boulders hold is the treasure. About 120 species of lichen grow here, and erosion from feet does real damage to them and to the mosses. That is why Natural England and the national park ask visitors to stay on the paths around the edge and not to go in. The view from the path is the visit.

The wood has been a Site of Special Scientific Interest since 1964 and is owned by the Duchy of Cornwall. A plan agreed in 2023 aims to cut grazing and foot traffic and let this rainforest spread by 2040.

View from the path at the edge. Roughly a 25 minute walk north from the Two Bridges car park on the B3357.

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a low, mossy wood of twisted oaks among granite boulders on the hillside above the West Dart. It is about a 25 minute walk north of the Two Bridges car park, seen from the path along its edge.
